Na pozostałym obszarze Śląska Cieszyńskiego ten typ akcentu występuje obocznie z typowym dla polszczyzny akcentem padającym na przedostatnią sylabę w wyrazie. new_statements.translation: In the south of Silesia, in the Jabłonków subdialect, initial stress occurs – on the first syllable of the word; this is a clear influence of the languages of the Czech-Slovak group. In the rest of Cieszyn Silesia this type of stress occurs side by side with the stress typical of Polish, falling on the penultimate syllable of the word. In the remaining Silesian area, as in the literary language, paroxytonic [penultimate] stress prevails.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable throughout the Silesian area, as in standard Polish. Malinowski 1873: 31 adds that in the Opole dialect this holds without exception ('stets'), even in -ija nouns (lelija, marija) where standard Polish has antepenultimate stress; Bystroń 1885: 29 says the same for the Cieszyn (Lachian) dialect ('zwykle na głoskę przedostatnią').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Jabłonków (Jablunkov) subdialect in the far south: initial stress (Czech/Slovak influence); elsewhere in Cieszyn Silesia initial stress alternates with penultimate (Winiarska). Bystroń 1885: 29-30: stress wavers in -ija/-yja loans (biblija, Maryja); Czech-borrowed 'poxvalen' stressed on 2nd or 3rd from end; fused phrases (svęntyjan, svatydux) take one penultimate stress; the question 'a vidźiś?' always has final stress and questions generally shift stress to the final vowel (pitch about a fifth higher). Nikel 1908: 12 notes stress on the -i- of loans in -ia/-io/-ium.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress; dialect descriptions of spoken varieties (Opole, Upper Silesian industrial district, Cieszyn/Zaolzie). The Winiarska page is a synthesizing dialect characterization in a multimedia dialectology guide, not a fieldwork monograph; the primary statements from Malinowski 1873 and Bystroń 1885 are 19th-century.
new_statements.identity_note: sile1253 = Silesian (szl), the Silesian dialect group of Lechitic. The deciding statement (Winiarska) covers the whole 'dialekt śląski' and singles out the Jabłonków (Jablunkov, CZ) subdialect with initial stress and the rest of Cieszyn Silesia with variable initial/penultimate stress. The corroborating primaries are sub-dialect specific: Malinowski 1873 = Opole (Oppeln) dialect, northern Silesia; Bystroń 1885 = 'gwara laska' of the Stonawka and Łucyna basins in Teschen Silesia (today Czech Zaolzie; a Cieszyn Silesian variety); Nikel 1908 = Upper Silesian industrial district (Zabrze/Bytom/Katowice). I did not extract Glottolog dialect codes for these subvarieties (the page's tree JSON failed to parse).

new_statements.quote: § 16. In den Lehnwörtern auf urspr. io, ion, ia, ium hat i stets den Ton und wird diphthongisch = ii̯ gesprochen, z. B. nacii̯á (ein Schimpfwort, etwa infamiger Kerl), pénzii̯á (Pension), v́ilii̯á (Vigil, hl. Abend), faḿilii̯á (Familie), ǵimnazii̯á (Gymnasium), Turcii̯á (Türkei), Francii̯á (Frankreich) usw. Ebenso verhalten sich auch die übrigen Lehnwörter auf -ia wie kanalii̯á (Canaille), metalii̯á (Medaille als Auszeichnung), fuzii̯á (Flinte), šampańii̯á (Champagner).
new_statements.translation: § 16. In loanwords in original io, ion, ia, ium the i always carries the stress and is pronounced as a diphthong = ii̯, e.g. nacii̯á (a term of abuse, roughly 'infamous fellow'), pénzii̯á (pension), v́ilii̯á (vigil, Christmas Eve), faḿilii̯á (family), ǵimnazii̯á (Gymnasium), Turcii̯á (Turkey), Francii̯á (France) etc. The remaining loanwords in -ia behave the same way, e.g. kanalii̯á (canaille), metalii̯á (medal as a decoration), fuzii̯á (rifle), šampańii̯á (champagne).
new_statements.citation: Nikel, Emanuel (1908). Die polnische Mundart des oberschlisischen Industriebezirks. Berlin: Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität zu Berlin. 48 pp.
new_statements.locator: § 16, printed p. 12 (PDF page 12); the sign key on p. 4 lists '| bez. die Tonsilbe' but the mark is never used in the running text

Sign key on printed p. 4 (PDF page 4, rendered and read): '| bez. die Tonsilbe…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate rule and with the Winiarska statement: it adds the detail that -ia/-ium loans are resyllabified as -ija with the stress on the i (penult), unlike Standard Polish which keeps them shorter. It does not state a general stress rule and says nothing about the initial stress of the Jabłonków subdialect (which lies outside Nikel's area anyway).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work has no accent/stress section (Teil I covers vowels, consonants and parts of inflection, §§ 1-62). Its only statement on stress is incidental: in loanwords ending in -io/-ion/-ia/-ium the i always bears the stress and the ending is disyllabic (-ii̯-á), so every example is stressed on the syllable before the final -a, i.e. on the penult of the dialect form (fa.mi.LII̯.á, pen.ZII̯.á, gim.na.ZII̯.á), where Standard Polish stresses the corresponding word on the penult of a shorter form (fa.MI.lja, PEN.sja). Penultimate stress is implied, not stated as a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the § 16 remark itself concerns only this loanword class. No other word in the text carries the stress mark from the sign key.
new_statements.identity_note: Nikel 1908 describes the Polish dialect of the Upper Silesian industrial district (Kreise Zabrze, Beuthen, Kattowitz and parts of Gleiwitz, Tarnowitz, Pless, Rybnik; Vorwort p. 3), i.e. the core Upper Silesian variety; only Teil I (Lautlehre and parts of the Formenlehre) was ever printed. The catalog's existing statement (Winiarska) covers the Silesian dialect area generally including Cieszyn Silesia.

(In the Lachian [Cieszyn/Teschen] subdialect stress falls, as in the general language, usually on the penultimate syllable.)
